sentences.text: Corythosaurus grew to a length of 7.7 to 9 meters, with a skull and crest standing 70.8 cm tall.
Proportionally, the skull of Corythosaurus is shorter and smaller than those of Edmontosaurus, Kritosaurus, or Saurolophus.
The sides and tail of the holotype were covered in various types of scales.
More than twenty skulls of Corythosaurus have been discovered.
Corythosaurus casuarius is one of the few lambeosaurines with surviving fossilized juveniles assigned to the species.
A Corythosaurus specimen was preserved with its last meal, consisting of conifer needles, seeds, twigs, and fruits, found in its chest cavity.
It is proven that Corythosaurus crests lacked holes and could not function for buoyancy, as water pressure at 3 meters would prevent lung inflation.
Scientists speculate Corythosaurus could produce loud, low-pitched calls resembling a trombone or wind instrument.
Corythosaurus emitted low-frequency sounds through its nasal passages when exhaling.
The genus Corythosaurus was described by Barnum Brown in 1914.
The genus Corythosaurus was named by Brown in 1914.
The holotype specimen AMNH 5240 was discovered in 1911 and secured in the fall of 1912 by Barnum Brown in Alberta.
The holotype specimen of Corythosaurus was found in the Belly River Group.
Barnum Brown identified specific characteristics in 1914 to distinguish Corythosaurus from other Alberta hadrosaurids.
Over fifty articulated specimens from many genera have been found in the Dinosaur Park Formation.
Corythosaurus was an ornithopod and therefore a herbivore.
Benson et al. (2012) concluded Corythosaurus fed on soft vegetation due to its shallow and delicate beak.
A preserved Corythosaurus specimen contained conifer needles, seeds, twigs, and fruits in its chest cavity, indicating it was a browser.
Benson et al. (2012) estimated the average length of Corythosaurus to be 9 meters.
Testing of a model concluded that the average weight of Corythosaurus was 3.82 tons.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Corythosaurus may have been cathemeral, active in short intervals throughout the day.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Corythosaurus may have been catemeral, active throughout the day in short intervals.
Corythosaurus likely possessed a sensitive middle ear, indicated by a thin stapes and large eardrum.
Researchers suggest the crest functioned for vocalization, acting like a trombone to amplify sound waves as the animal exhaled.
Although once thought to be semi-aquatic due to webbed feet, the 'webs' were actually deflated padding similar to modern mammals.
The holotype specimen was found as a carcass that had floated onto a beach, surrounded by water-worn bones and shells.
Dudgeon, Brown, and Evans (2026) described the internal crest anatomy of mature Corythosaurus individuals.
Corythosaurus is classified as a hadrosaurid dinosaur within the subfamily Lambeosaurinae.
Corythosaurus is classified as a lambeosaurine, related to Lambeosaurus, Nipponosaurus, Velafrons, Hypacrosaurus, and Olorotitan.
Fossils of Corythosaurus have been found in the Oldman and Dinosaur Park Formations in Canada.
Corythosaurus lived approximately 77 to 75.7 million years ago.
Corythosaurus lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
It is debated regarding the exact structure of the crest, as Barnum Brown incorrectly identified the praemaxillae as nasals.
Many presumed traits of the snout described by Brown are incorrect due to confusion between bone types.
Earlier paleontologists recognized four genera and thirteen species in the Dinosaur Park Formation based on size and crest shape differences, a classification now largely revised.
